title: Platforms for Humans and Machines: Engineering for the Age of Agents — Juan Herreros Elorza

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 83%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is about building internal developer platforms (Atlas) that serve both human engineers and AI coding agents as first-class users. The platform serves software builders at a financial services company, fitting the developer platforms domain. The discussion concerns production platform engineering practices for operating and maintaining internal developer platforms. The content assumes familiarity with platform engineering, APIs, Kubernetes, and CI/CD but remains accessible to practitioners. This is a conference talk presented at AI Engineer with structured slides and a single speaker. All claims are directly stated by the speaker in the transcript with no external verification.

summary: Juan Herreros Elorza from Banking Circle presents on building internal developer platforms that work for both humans and AI coding agents. Banking Circle is a fintech processing over 1 trillion euro per year with 250+ engineers, whose internal platform Atlas spans compute (Kubernetes), infrastructure provisioning (blob storage, databases, secrets), messaging, and observability. Juan opens with a fictionalized but experience-based story: a new developer builds an application, then struggles to deploy it—copying pipelines, hitting failures, being redirected to infrastructure teammates, waiting for help, and discovering missing dependencies. This painful workflow was always bad for humans but is essentially impossible for AI agents, which cannot walk to another floor or casually ask a colleague. The core thesis is that best practices remain best practices—they are just more obvious and more painful now that agents work alongside developers. Juan identifies several key principles. First, self-service is essential: no process should require talking to or waiting for a specific person. Second, platforms should be API-based with well-defined, discoverable APIs featuring schema validation and authentication; CLIs or MCP servers can sit on top. Third, local-first workflows matter: shift left so failures happen as early as possible on the developer's machine. Fourth, observability must be agent-accessible via APIs, CLIs, or MCP servers—not just graphical dashboards. Fifth, documentation must be structured and strategically placed, either co-located with code or centralized for platform-wide docs, and delivered via API rather than whole HTML pages. Agent-specific documentation files like agents.md can describe how agents should work in a repository, and skills (markdown documents) can codify conventions for specific task types. Juan also encourages contributions to platforms since AI lowers the entry barrier, but warns this is a double-edged sword requiring guardrails—policies for hard constraints plus markdown context files for guidance. Measuring success is critical: use DORA metrics for delivery, reliability metrics, platform-specific metrics like support request volume, and frameworks like SPACE for developer satisfaction. Finally, Juan suggests using the current AI momentum as an excuse to implement best practices that previously met organizational resistance.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Banking Circle Context
sections.summary: Juan introduces himself and Banking Circle, a cross-border payments provider processing over 1 trillion euro annually with 700+ regulated financial institutions. He explains the company established a platform engineering team to support 250+ engineers building APIs, core banking systems, internal tools, data systems, and clearing integrations.

sections.title: Atlas Platform Overview
sections.summary: The internal platform Atlas comprises sub-platforms for compute (Kubernetes), infrastructure (blob storage, databases, secrets), messaging, and observability, designed to abstract infrastructure complexity so teams can focus on building their systems.

sections.title: Developer Deployment Frustration Story
sections.summary: Juan tells a fictionalized story of a new developer who builds an application but struggles to deploy it—copying pipelines, hitting failures, being redirected to infrastructure teammates, waiting for help, and discovering missing dependencies like databases. This situation is frustrating for humans and impossible for AI agents.

sections.title: Best Practices Are Still Best Practices
sections.summary: Juan states that relying on teammates, waiting for pipelines, and informal cross-team coordination were never good practices—they are simply more obvious and painful now that coding agents work alongside developers.

sections.title: Self-Service Principle
sections.summary: Self-service is the first principle: both developers and agents must be able to do everything on the platform independently, with no dependency on specific people. The self-service flow must also be intuitive and automatic, not a patchwork of steps from scattered sources.

sections.title: API-Based Platform Access
sections.summary: Platforms should expose well-defined, discoverable APIs with schema validation and authentication. CLIs or MCP servers can sit on top, but the API foundation lets agents loop, receive responses, and iterate until they succeed in a secure way.

sections.title: Local-First Workflows and Shift Left
sections.summary: Since agents run locally, platforms should shift left so failures happen as early as possible—ideally on the developer's machine—rather than after pushing to version control. Agents can then iterate locally until they meet clearly defined success criteria.

sections.title: Observability for Agents
sections.summary: Observability must be agent-accessible. Logs, metrics, and traces should be available via APIs, CLIs, or MCP servers, not just graphical dashboards, so agents can close the loop and verify task completion programmatically.

sections.title: Documentation Strategies
sections.summary: Documentation must be structured for agent consumption. For smaller repos, keep docs next to the code they document. For platform-wide documentation, centralize it so agents can discover and use it effectively.

sections.title: API-First Documentation and Agent-Specific Docs
sections.summary: Juan recommends delivering documentation via API so agents receive only relevant bits rather than entire HTML pages. He introduces agent-specific documentation files like agents.md or compiler_instructions.md, which describe how an agent should build, test, deploy, and verify in a particular repository. These can be layered—general ones applying across systems plus specific ones per project. Skills, which are markdown documents codifying conventions, can guide agents on how to perform specific task types.

sections.title: Encouraging Contributions with Guardrails
sections.summary: Juan encourages contributions to internal platforms since AI agents lower the entry barrier for developers. However, this is a double-edged sword because platform owners remain responsible for maintenance. He recommends a combination approach: enforce policies as hard guardrails for security, compliance, and standards, while using markdown files like agents.md and skills to guide agents on how to contribute in the desired way.

sections.title: Measuring Platform Success
sections.summary: Juan emphasizes measuring whether platform changes actually work. He references DORA metrics (change frequency, mean time to recovery, lead time) for application delivery, reliability metrics especially important in fintech, platform-specific metrics like support request volume, and developer satisfaction frameworks like SPACE. The key point is to define what you want to achieve and measure whether you succeeded.

sections.title: Summary and Closing Advice
sections.summary: Juan summarizes his advice: make platforms self-service, API-based, and local-first; ensure good documentation and observability; encourage contributions; and measure results. He adds a final tip: use the current AI momentum at all organizational levels as an excuse to implement best practices that previously met resistance. He closes with links to his LinkedIn, personal website, and GitHub.
